title: Part 2, Chapter 56
paragraphs: The prodigious and unparalleled battle that took place between Don Quixote of La Mancha and the lacquey Tosilos in defence of the daughter of Doña Rodriguez

The duke and duchess had no reason to regret the joke played on Sancho Panza in giving him the government, especially as their majordomo returned the same day and gave them a minute account of nearly every word and deed Sancho uttered or did during the time; and to wind up with, eloquently described the attack on the island and Sancho's fright and departure, all of which amused them a great deal. After this the history goes on to say that the day fixed for the battle arrived, and that the duke, after repeatedly instructing his lacquey Tosilos how to deal with Don Quixote so as to vanquish him without killing or wounding him, gave orders to have the heads removed from the lances, telling Don Quixote that Christian charity, on which he prided himself, could not allow the battle to be fought with so much risk and danger to life, and that he must be content with the offer of a battlefield on his territory (though that was against the decree of the holy Council, which prohibits all challenges of the sort) and not push such an arduous venture to its extreme. Don Quixote bid his excellence arrange every detail of the affair as he pleased, since for his part he would obey him in everything. The dread day having arrived, then, and the duke having ordered a spacious stand to be set up facing the castle courtyard for the judges of the field and the appellant duennas, mother and daughter, vast crowds streamed in from all the villages and hamlets of the neighbourhood to see the novel spectacle of the battle; nobody, dead or alive, in those parts had ever seen or heard of one like it.

The first to enter the field and the lists was the master of ceremonies, who surveyed and paced the whole ground to see that there was nothing unfair and nothing concealed that might make the combatants stumble or fall; then the duennas entered and took their seats, wrapped in mantles that covered their eyes — even their bosoms — and displaying no slight emotion as Don Quixote appeared in the lists. Shortly afterwards, accompanied by several trumpets and mounted on a powerful steed that looked like it would crush the whole place, the great lacquey Tosilos made his appearance on one side of the courtyard with his visor down, stiffly cased in a suit of stout, shining armour. The horse was plainly a Frieslander, broad-backed and dapple-grey, with half a pound of wool hanging from each fetlock. The gallant combatant came well primed by his master the duke as to how he was to behave against the valiant Don Quixote of La Mancha, warned that he must on no account kill him, but should try to shirk the first encounter to avoid the risk of killing him, as he was sure to do if he met him full tilt. He crossed the courtyard at a walk, and reaching the spot where the duennas were placed stopped to look at the one who demanded him for a husband. The marshal of the field summoned Don Quixote, who had already presented himself in the courtyard, and standing by Tosilos's side he addressed the duennas and asked if they consented that Don Quixote of La Mancha should do battle for their right. They said they did, and that whatever he did on their behalf they declared rightly done, final, and valid. By this time the duke and duchess had taken their places in a gallery overlooking the enclosure, which was packed to overflowing with a multitude eager to see this perilous and unparalleled encounter. The conditions of the combat were that if Don Quixote proved the victor, his opponent was to marry the daughter of Doña Rodriguez; but if he should be vanquished, his opponent was released from the promise that was claimed against him and from all obligation to give satisfaction. The master of ceremonies divided the sun between them and stationed them, each on the spot where he was to stand. The drums beat, the sound of the trumpets filled the air, the earth trembled underfoot, the hearts of the watching crowd were full of suspense, some hoping for a happy outcome, some apprehensive of an untoward ending; and at last Don Quixote, commending himself with all his heart to God our Lord and to the lady Dulcinea del Toboso, stood waiting for the signal for the onset. Our lacquey, however, was thinking of something very different; he was thinking only of what I am now about to tell.

It seems that as he stood contemplating his enemy she struck him as the most beautiful woman he had ever seen in his life; and the little blind boy whom in our streets they commonly call Love had no mind to let slip the chance of triumphing over a lacquey heart and adding it to his trophies. So, stealing gently up on him unseen, he drove a dart two yards long into the poor lacquey's left side and pierced his heart through and through — which he was able to do quite at his ease, for Love is invisible, and comes in and goes out as he likes, without anyone calling him to account for what he does. Well then, when they gave the signal for the onset our lacquey was in an ecstasy, musing on the beauty of her whom he had already made mistress of his liberty, and so he paid no attention to the trumpet, unlike Don Quixote, who was off the instant he heard it and, at the highest speed Rocinante could manage, set off to meet his enemy. His good squire Sancho shouted lustily as he saw him start, "God guide you, cream and flower of knights-errant! God give you the victory, for the right is on your side!" But although Tosilos saw Don Quixote coming at him, he never stirred a step from the spot where he was posted; instead, he called loudly to the marshal of the field, and when the marshal came up to see what he wanted, Tosilos said, "Señor, isn't this battle to decide whether I marry or do not marry that lady?" "Just so," was the answer. "Well then," said the lacquey, "I feel qualms of conscience, and I'd put a heavy burden on it if I went any further with the combat; so I declare that I yield myself vanquished and that I am willing to marry the lady at once."

The marshal of the field was lost in astonishment at Tosilos's words; and as he was one of those who were in on the arrangement of the affair, he didn't know what to say in reply. Don Quixote pulled up in mid-career when he saw that his enemy was not coming on to the attack. The duke couldn't make out why the battle wasn't going on, but the marshal of the field hurried over to let him know what Tosilos had said, and he was amazed and extremely angry at it. Meanwhile Tosilos advanced to where Doña Rodriguez sat and said in a loud voice, "Señora, I am willing to marry your daughter, and I have no wish to obtain by strife and fighting what I can obtain in peace and without any risk to my life."

The valiant Don Quixote heard him and said, "As that is the case I am released and absolved from my promise; let them marry by all means, and as 'God our Lord has given her, may Saint Peter add his blessing.'"

The duke had now come down to the castle courtyard, and going up to Tosilos he said, "Is it true, sir knight, that you yield yourself vanquished, and that out of scruples of conscience you wish to marry this damsel?"
"And he does well," said Sancho, "for what you have to give to the mouse, give to the cat, and it will save you all the trouble."

Tosilos meanwhile was trying to unlace his helmet, and he begged them to come to his help at once, as he was running short of breath and could not remain so long shut up in that confined space. They removed it in haste, and his lacquey features were revealed to public view. At this sight Doña Rodriguez and her daughter raised a mighty outcry, exclaiming, "This is a trick! This is a trick! They have put Tosilos, my lord the duke's lacquey, on us in place of the real husband. The justice of God and the king against such trickery — not to say roguery!"

"Do not distress yourselves, ladies," said Don Quixote; "this is no trickery or roguery, or if it is, it is not the duke who is at the bottom of it but those wicked enchanters who persecute me, and who, jealous of my reaping the glory of this victory, have turned your husband's features into those of this person, who you say is the duke's lacquey. Take my advice, and despite the malice of my enemies marry him, for beyond a doubt he is the one you want for a husband."

When the duke heard this his anger all but vanished in a fit of laughter, and he said, "The things that happen to Señor Don Quixote are so extraordinary that I am ready to believe this lacquey of mine is not one; but let us adopt this plan and stratagem: let us put off the marriage for, say, a fortnight, and let us keep this person we are uncertain about in close confinement, and perhaps in the course of that time he may return to his original shape; for the spite the enchanters bear Señor Don Quixote can't last so long, especially as it is of so little benefit to them to practise these deceptions and transformations."

"Oh, señor," said Sancho, "those scoundrels are well used to changing whatever concerns my master from one thing into another. A knight he overcame some time back, called the Knight of the Mirrors, they turned into the shape of the bachelor Sansón Carrasco of our town and a great friend of ours; and my lady Dulcinea del Toboso they have turned into a common country girl; so I suspect this lacquey will have to live and die a lacquey all the days of his life."

Here Rodriguez's daughter exclaimed, "Whoever this man is who claims me for a wife, I am thankful to him for it, for I'd rather be the lawful wife of a lacquey than the cheated mistress of a gentleman — though the one who played me false was no real gentleman either."

To be brief, all the talk and all that had happened ended in Tosilos being shut up until it was seen how his transformation turned out. All hailed Don Quixote as victor, but the greater number were vexed and disappointed to find that the combatants they had been so anxiously waiting for had not battered one another to pieces — just as boys are disappointed when the man they are waiting to see hanged does not come out because the prosecution or the court has pardoned him. The crowd dispersed, the duke and Don Quixote returned to the castle, Tosilos was locked up, Doña Rodriguez and her daughter remained perfectly contented to see that the affair must end in a marriage one way or another, and Tosilos wanted nothing else.
